title: A/B Testing
tagline: The structured way companies test whether a change actually works — or just feels like it does.
what_it_is: An A/B test is a controlled experiment where you randomly split users into two groups, show each group a different version of something, and measure which performs better. Group A gets the current version (control). Group B gets the changed version (treatment). Statistics then tells you whether any difference you observe is real or just random noise.
key_points: Random assignment is non-negotiable. Without it, you can't establish causation — only correlation.
Run a power calculation first to know how long to run the test before starting.
Pick one primary metric before the test. Checking many metrics and picking the winner is p-hacking.
Don't stop the test early just because you see a significant result — early significance is often a fluke.
Practical significance (effect size) matters as much as statistical significance. A 0.01% lift that's significant isn't worth shipping.
why_it_exists: Our intuition about what will work is frequently wrong. A redesigned button that looks better to the designer might perform worse for users. A clunkier checkout flow might actually increase conversions. A/B testing is the antidote to HiPPO decisions — Highest Paid Person's Opinion. It lets data decide instead of gut feel.
intuition: Imagine a restaurant wants to know if a new menu layout increases orders of the daily special. Option 1: just switch the menu and see if specials sales go up. But what if sales went up because of a local event that week? Or a competitor closed? You can't separate the menu effect from everything else happening at the same time. Option 2: on the same day, half the tables get the new menu and half get the old one. Tables are assigned randomly. Now everything else is the same — the only difference is the menu. Any sales difference between the two groups has to be because of the menu. That isolation of cause is what an A/B test gives you.

steps.title: Define the hypothesis
steps.description: Be specific. Not 'will the new button perform better?' but 'will changing the CTA button from grey to orange increase clicks by at least 5%?' Name your primary metric. Name your minimum detectable effect.

steps.title: Run a power calculation
steps.description: Based on your baseline conversion rate, minimum detectable effect, alpha (typically 0.05), and target power (typically 0.80) — calculate the minimum sample size per group. This tells you how long to run the test.

steps.title: Randomise assignment
steps.description: Every user must be randomly assigned to control or treatment — not by device type, not by signup date, not by country. Random. Consistent (same user always sees the same variant).

steps.title: Run the test for the pre-specified duration
steps.description: Don't peek and stop early. Don't extend when you're close. Commit to the sample size you calculated. This is the hardest part in practice.

steps.title: Analyse the result
steps.description: Run your chosen statistical test (usually a two-proportion z-test for conversion rates). Check p-value against alpha. Then check effect size — is the lift large enough to matter? Then ship or don't.

visual.description: A flowchart showing: users enter → random split → 50% see Control (A), 50% see Treatment (B) → both groups measured on the same metric → statistical test applied → decision: ship or don't. Annotate each step with what can go wrong if done incorrectly (e.g., non-random split = selection bias, peeking early = inflated alpha).

when_to_use: When you want to establish causation, not just observe a correlation
When you have enough traffic or users to reach the required sample size in a reasonable time
When there's one clear primary metric and a meaningful minimum effect size to detect
when_not_to_use: When you can't randomise — you can't run a proper A/B test on a policy change that affects everyone at once
When traffic is too low — if you need 50,000 users per group and only get 500/day, the test takes years
When the change has strong network effects — showing half the users a new social feature while others don't see it creates contamination between groups
common_mistakes: Peeking at results and stopping early when p < 0.05 appears — this inflates false positive rates dramatically. If you must peek, use sequential testing methods.
Testing too many variants at once without adjusting for multiple comparisons — A vs B vs C vs D is not 3 separate A/B tests
Forgetting the novelty effect — users sometimes engage more with anything new, regardless of quality. The lift may fade after a few weeks.
Using non-representative samples — if you test only on mobile users in the US, the result may not generalise to desktop users in Europe
notes: In industry, A/B tests are sometimes called 'controlled experiments', 'randomized controlled trials' (RCTs), or just 'experiments'. Same thing.

Bayesian A/B testing is an increasingly popular alternative. Instead of waiting for a fixed sample size and getting a p-value, you get a continuous probability that one variant is better — and can stop when confidence is high enough. Covered in Bayesian Thinking.
ds_usage: A/B testing is the backbone of product development at tech companies. Google runs thousands simultaneously. The data science role includes: designing the experiment, calculating required sample sizes, monitoring for data quality issues (SRM — sample ratio mismatch), running the statistical analysis, and communicating results. Tools: Optimizely, LaunchDarkly, Statsig, and custom internal experimentation platforms.
